category: Nouns that are countable and uncountable — with different meanings

entries.meaning: The threadlike growth on the head and body.
examples: Her hair is longer than it used to be.
He's losing his hair.
She washed her hair twice.
There's a hair in my soup.
Two hairs were recovered from the scene.
He pulled a gray hair out and threw it away.
Let your hair down for once.
That was a hair-raising drive.
She won by a hair.

senses.head: The mass on someone's head
examples: Her hair is longer than it used to be.
He's losing his hair.
She washed her hair twice.

senses.head: A single strand
examples: There's a hair in my soup.
Two hairs were recovered from the scene.
He pulled a gray hair out and threw it away.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: Let your hair down for once.
That was a hair-raising drive.
She won by a hair.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a mass, countable as single strands
entries.agreement: singular verb for the mass — her hair is long; plural for strands — two hairs were found
entries.counted with: a strand of hair, a lock of hair, a head of hair
entries.contrast: This is the textbook case. She has beautiful hair — the mass on her head. There's a hair in my food — one strand. Saying ✗ she has beautiful hairs describes something disturbing.

entries.meaning: The transparent material; a drinking vessel; spectacles.
examples: The whole wall is glass.
Broken glass covered the sidewalk.
The window pane is toughened glass.
Pour me a glass of water.
All the glasses are in the dishwasher.
He knocked a glass off the table.
I can't read without my glasses.

senses.head: The material
examples: The whole wall is glass.
Broken glass covered the sidewalk.
The window pane is toughened glass.

senses.head: A drinking vessel
examples: Pour me a glass of water.
All the glasses are in the dishwasher.
He knocked a glass off the table.

senses.head: Spectacles — glasses
examples: I can't read without my glasses.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a material, countable as a vessel
entries.agreement: singular for the material — the glass is toughened; plural for vessels — the glasses are clean
entries.counted with: a pane of glass, a sheet of glass, a piece of glass
entries.variants: glasses also means spectacles, and in that sense is plural-only — see glasses
entries.contrast: Three grammars in one word. The material is uncountable; a drinking vessel is countable; and glasses meaning spectacles is a plural-only noun that takes a plural verb and no singular.

entries.meaning: The material; a newspaper; a written document.
examples: We're out of paper.
Bring me a sheet of paper.
The report was printed on heavy paper.
He reads the paper every morning.
Both local papers covered the story.
She published three papers last year.
The paper is due on Monday.
The border guard asked for our papers.

senses.head: The material
examples: We're out of paper.
Bring me a sheet of paper.
The report was printed on heavy paper.

senses.head: A newspaper
examples: He reads the paper every morning.
Both local papers covered the story.

senses.head: An academic article or essay
examples: She published three papers last year.
The paper is due on Monday.

senses.head: Official documents — papers
examples: The border guard asked for our papers.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a material, countable as a document
entries.agreement: singular for the material — the paper is thin; plural for documents — the papers are due
entries.counted with: a sheet of paper, a piece of paper, a ream of paper
entries.contrast: ✗ Give me a paper meaning a blank sheet is wrong — say a sheet of paper or a piece of paper. A paper means a newspaper, an academic article, or an exam.

entries.meaning: The hard material from trees; a small forest.
examples: The table is solid wood.
We need more wood for the fire.
He carved it from a single piece of wood.
They walked in the woods all afternoon.
The woods behind the house are full of deer.
We're not out of the woods yet.
Knock on wood.

senses.head: The material
examples: The table is solid wood.
We need more wood for the fire.
He carved it from a single piece of wood.

senses.head: A forest
examples: They walked in the woods all afternoon.
The woods behind the house are full of deer.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: We're not out of the woods yet.
Knock on wood.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a material, countable as a forest
entries.agreement: singular for the material — the wood is dry; plural for forests — the woods are dark
entries.counted with: a piece of wood, a plank of wood, a log
entries.variants: woods usually means a small forest, and is used as a plural even for one
entries.contrast: ✗ a wood for a piece of timber is wrong — say a piece of wood. In American English the woods means the forest, and takes a plural verb even when one forest is meant: the woods are quiet.

entries.meaning: The metal; the appliance for pressing clothes.
examples: The gate is made of wrought iron.
Iron rusts quickly in salt air.
She's low on iron and needs supplements.
The iron is still hot.
Both travel irons stopped working.
Strike while the iron is hot.
He has several irons in the fire.

senses.head: The metal
examples: The gate is made of wrought iron.
Iron rusts quickly in salt air.
She's low on iron and needs supplements.

senses.head: The pressing appliance
examples: The iron is still hot.
Both travel irons stopped working.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: Strike while the iron is hot.
He has several irons in the fire.

entries.pronunciation note: the r comes before the vowel sound
entries.countability: both — uncountable as a metal, countable as an appliance
entries.agreement: singular for the metal — iron is heavy; plural for appliances — both irons are broken
entries.counted with: a bar of iron, a piece of iron
entries.contrast: The pronunciation is the trap: EYE-urn, not ✗ EYE-ron. The metal is uncountable, the pressing appliance countable, and irons also means shackles.

entries.meaning: The drink and the beans it is made from.
examples: The coffee has gone cold.
Do you want some coffee?
We're out of coffee again.
Two coffees, please.
She's already had three coffees today.
There's a coffee shop on every corner.

senses.head: The drink or the substance
examples: The coffee has gone cold.
Do you want some coffee?
We're out of coffee again.

senses.head: A serving of coffee
examples: Two coffees, please.
She's already had three coffees today.

senses.head: Attributive
examples: There's a coffee shop on every corner.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a substance, countable as a serving
entries.agreement: singular for the drink — the coffee is cold; plural for servings — two coffees, please
entries.counted with: a cup of coffee, a pot of coffee, a bag of coffee
entries.contrast: Ordering two coffees is completely normal English — the countable sense means servings. But ✗ I spilled a coffee on the carpet meaning the liquid is odd; say some coffee. The same double life belongs to tea, beer, and wine.

entries.meaning: The bird, and its meat.
examples: They keep six chickens in the backyard.
A chicken got loose in the road.
We're having chicken for dinner.
The chicken is a little dry.
Add two pieces of chicken to the pan.
Don't be such a chicken.

senses.head: The living bird
examples: They keep six chickens in the backyard.
A chicken got loose in the road.

senses.head: The meat
examples: We're having chicken for dinner.
The chicken is a little dry.
Add two pieces of chicken to the pan.

senses.head: A coward
examples: Don't be such a chicken.

entries.countability: both — countable as the animal, uncountable as the meat
entries.agreement: singular for the meat — the chicken is overcooked; plural for birds — the chickens are in the yard
entries.counted with: a piece of chicken, a breast of chicken
entries.contrast: This animal/meat split is one of the most systematic patterns in English. Live birds are countable; the meat is uncountable. ✗ I ate a chicken means you ate an entire bird. Compare lamb, fish, turkey, and duck, which work the same way — and cow/beef, pig/pork, sheep/mutton, where English uses different words entirely.

entries.meaning: Duration; an occasion; a point in the day.
examples: We don't have much time.
Time passes slowly here.
It takes a lot of time to learn.
I've seen it three times.
The first time was the worst.
How many times do I have to ask?
In Roman times this was a garrison town.
What time is it?

senses.head: Duration
examples: We don't have much time.
Time passes slowly here.
It takes a lot of time to learn.

senses.head: An occasion
examples: I've seen it three times.
The first time was the worst.
How many times do I have to ask?

senses.head: A period in history
examples: In Roman times this was a garrison town.

senses.head: A point in the day
examples: What time is it?

entries.countability: both — uncountable as duration, countable as occasions
entries.agreement: singular for duration — time is short; plural for occasions — three times were recorded
entries.counted with: a period of time, an amount of time
entries.contrast: The two senses take different question words. How much time? asks about duration; how many times? asks about occasions. Mixing them — ✗ how much times — is a very common error.

entries.meaning: A part of a building; also available space.
examples: The house has four rooms upstairs.
She booked a room for two nights.
Which room is the meeting in?
Is there room for one more?
There isn't enough room in the trunk.
Make room on the table.
There's room for improvement.

senses.head: A part of a building
examples: The house has four rooms upstairs.
She booked a room for two nights.
Which room is the meeting in?

senses.head: Available space
examples: Is there room for one more?
There isn't enough room in the trunk.
Make room on the table.

senses.head: Scope or opportunity
examples: There's room for improvement.

entries.countability: both — countable as a space in a building, uncountable as available space
entries.agreement: singular for space — there is room for one more; plural for rooms — the rooms are booked
entries.counted with: a lot of room, plenty of room
entries.contrast: ✗ There is a room for one more person means a bedroom is available. Without the article it means space is available. The difference matters at a hotel desk.

entries.meaning: Extent or area; the universe beyond Earth; a defined area.
examples: There's not enough space on the shelf.
Space in the city is expensive.
I found a parking space two blocks away.
All the spaces are reserved.
They rent office space downtown.
The telescope was launched into space.

senses.head: Available extent
examples: There's not enough space on the shelf.
Space in the city is expensive.

senses.head: A defined area
examples: I found a parking space two blocks away.
All the spaces are reserved.
They rent office space downtown.

senses.head: The universe beyond Earth
examples: The telescope was launched into space.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as extent, countable as a defined area
entries.agreement: singular for extent — space is limited; plural for areas — the spaces are numbered
entries.counted with: an amount of space, a lot of space
entries.contrast: ✗ a space meaning the universe is wrong — that sense is always uncountable and takes no article: travel in space, never ✗ in the space.

entries.meaning: Accumulated knowledge from doing something; also a single event lived through.
examples: The job requires five years' experience.
She has a lot of experience with this software.
Experience counts more than qualifications here.
It was a terrifying experience.
Those early experiences shaped everything he wrote.
Living abroad was a valuable experience.

senses.head: Accumulated knowledge or skill
examples: The job requires five years' experience.
She has a lot of experience with this software.
Experience counts more than qualifications here.

senses.head: A single event lived through
examples: It was a terrifying experience.
Those early experiences shaped everything he wrote.
Living abroad was a valuable experience.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as accumulated knowledge, countable as a single event
entries.agreement: singular for the mass — experience is essential; plural for events — those experiences shaped her
entries.counted with: a piece of experience is unnatural — use years of experience
entries.contrast: ✗ He has many experiences in marketing means he lived through many marketing events, not that he is experienced. For qualifications say a lot of experience — uncountable.

entries.meaning: Commercial activity; a company; a matter to be dealt with.
examples: Business has been slow this quarter.
They do a lot of business in Asia.
He's in New York on business.
She runs a small business.
Several businesses closed on that block.
That's none of your business.
Let's get down to business.

senses.head: Commercial activity
examples: Business has been slow this quarter.
They do a lot of business in Asia.
He's in New York on business.

senses.head: A company
examples: She runs a small business.
Several businesses closed on that block.

senses.head: A matter or affair
examples: That's none of your business.
Let's get down to business.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as commerce, countable as a company
entries.agreement: singular for commerce — business is slow; plural for companies — the businesses closed
entries.counted with: a piece of business, a line of business
entries.contrast: The pronunciation drops the middle syllable — BIZ-nis, not ✗ BIZ-ee-nis. Commerce in general is uncountable; an individual company is countable.

entries.meaning: Labor; a task; a created piece of art or writing.
examples: There's too much work and not enough time.
She's at work until six.
Good work takes time.
His early works are the best.
It is a work of extraordinary ambition.
The steel works closed in 1982.
The whole thing is a work in progress.
She threw a wrench in the works.

senses.head: Labor or employment
examples: There's too much work and not enough time.
She's at work until six.
Good work takes time.

senses.head: Artistic or literary creations
examples: His early works are the best.
It is a work of extraordinary ambition.

senses.head: A factory or industrial site — works
examples: The steel works closed in 1982.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The whole thing is a work in progress.
She threw a wrench in the works.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as labor, countable as a created piece
entries.agreement: singular for labor — the work is finished; plural for creations — his works are in three museums
entries.counted with: a piece of work, a job, a task
entries.contrast: ✗ I have many works to do is wrong — say a lot of work or many jobs. The countable works means artistic or literary creations, and separately a factory or mechanism.

entries.meaning: Illumination; a lamp or other source of it.
examples: There isn't enough light to read by.
Light travels faster than sound.
The room gets good light in the morning.
Turn the lights off when you leave.
One light is out in the hallway.
He stopped at a red light.
It puts the whole affair in a different light.
There's light at the end of the tunnel.

senses.head: Illumination
examples: There isn't enough light to read by.
Light travels faster than sound.
The room gets good light in the morning.

senses.head: A lamp or fixture
examples: Turn the lights off when you leave.
One light is out in the hallway.
He stopped at a red light.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: It puts the whole affair in a different light.
There's light at the end of the tunnel.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as illumination, countable as a lamp
entries.agreement: singular for illumination — the light is fading; plural for lamps — the lights are on
entries.counted with: a beam of light, a ray of light
entries.contrast: ✗ Turn off the light is fine if you mean one lamp, but turn off the lights is far commoner. The illumination sense takes no article and no plural.

entries.meaning: Sound, especially loud or unwanted sound.
examples: The noise from the street is constant.
There was too much noise to hear anything.
Try to make less noise coming in.
The engine is making strange noises.
I heard a noise in the kitchen.
He's been making noises about quitting.

senses.head: Unwanted sound generally
examples: The noise from the street is constant.
There was too much noise to hear anything.
Try to make less noise coming in.

senses.head: Individual sounds
examples: The engine is making strange noises.
I heard a noise in the kitchen.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: He's been making noises about quitting.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as unwanted sound, countable as a distinct sound
entries.agreement: singular for the mass — the noise is constant; plural for distinct sounds — strange noises were coming from the engine
entries.counted with: a lot of noise, a burst of noise
entries.contrast: Unwanted sound in general is uncountable; individual identifiable sounds are countable. There's a lot of noise versus the car is making strange noises — both correct, different meanings.

entries.meaning: Vibrations that can be heard.
examples: Sound travels faster in water.
The room was designed to absorb sound.
Turn the sound down.
She loves the sound of rain on the roof.
Strange sounds came from the basement.
He can imitate any sound you name.

senses.head: The phenomenon
examples: Sound travels faster in water.
The room was designed to absorb sound.
Turn the sound down.

senses.head: A particular thing heard
examples: She loves the sound of rain on the roof.
Strange sounds came from the basement.
He can imitate any sound you name.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the phenomenon, countable as a particular sound
entries.agreement: singular for the phenomenon — sound travels slowly; plural for particular ones — the sounds were recorded
entries.counted with: a burst of sound
entries.contrast: Compare noise: sound is neutral, noise is usually unwanted. The sound of rain is pleasant; the noise of rain suggests it is keeping you awake.

entries.meaning: Physical harm; in law, money awarded as compensation.
examples: The damage was worse than it looked.
Flooding caused extensive damage.
There's no permanent damage.
She sued for damages.
The jury awarded damages of four million dollars.
The lawyers went into damage control immediately.

senses.head: Physical or other harm
examples: The damage was worse than it looked.
Flooding caused extensive damage.
There's no permanent damage.

senses.head: Money awarded in court — damages
examples: She sued for damages.
The jury awarded damages of four million dollars.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The lawyers went into damage control immediately.

entries.countability: uncountable as harm; the plural damages means money awarded in court
entries.agreement: singular for harm — the damage is extensive; plural for compensation — damages were awarded
entries.counted with: an amount of damage, a lot of damage
entries.contrast: ✗ damages meaning physical harm is wrong — the plural has an entirely separate legal meaning: money paid in compensation. The storm caused a lot of damage versus the court awarded damages of two million dollars.

entries.meaning: Creative work; a skill; the creative disciplines.
examples: Art is more subjective than people admit.
She studied art in Rome.
The museum holds a great deal of modern art.
Conversation is a dying art.
He has the art of making people relax.
The arts are chronically underfunded.

senses.head: Creative work generally
examples: Art is more subjective than people admit.
She studied art in Rome.
The museum holds a great deal of modern art.

senses.head: A skill or knack
examples: Conversation is a dying art.
He has the art of making people relax.

senses.head: The creative disciplines — the arts
examples: The arts are chronically underfunded.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a field, countable as a skill or discipline
entries.agreement: singular for the field — art is subjective; plural for disciplines — the arts are underfunded
entries.counted with: a work of art, a piece of art
entries.contrast: ✗ An art meaning a painting is wrong — say a work of art. The arts means the creative disciplines collectively, and an art means a skill: the art of conversation.

entries.meaning: The quality of being beautiful; a beautiful person or thing.
examples: Beauty is famously subjective.
There is real beauty in the simplicity of it.
That car is an absolute beauty.
The guidebook lists the beauties of the coast.
The beauty of it is that nobody has to move.

senses.head: The quality
examples: Beauty is famously subjective.
There is real beauty in the simplicity of it.

senses.head: A beautiful thing or person
examples: That car is an absolute beauty.
The guidebook lists the beauties of the coast.

senses.head: An advantage
examples: The beauty of it is that nobody has to move.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a quality, countable as a beautiful thing
entries.agreement: singular for the quality — beauty is subjective; plural for things — the beauties of the region
entries.counted with: a thing of beauty
entries.contrast: The abstract quality is uncountable; a beautiful person or thing is countable. That car is a beauty is standard informal American.

entries.meaning: Conformity to fact; a fact accepted as true.
examples: Tell me the truth.
There is some truth in what he says.
Truth matters more than winning the argument.
We hold these truths to be self-evident.
The book contains some hard truths about the industry.

senses.head: The concept
examples: Tell me the truth.
There is some truth in what he says.
Truth matters more than winning the argument.

senses.head: A proposition held to be true
examples: We hold these truths to be self-evident.
The book contains some hard truths about the industry.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as a concept, countable as a proposition
entries.agreement: singular for the concept — truth matters; plural for propositions — these truths are self-evident
entries.counted with: a piece of the truth
entries.contrast: The concept is uncountable and usually takes the: tell the truth. A specific proposition held to be true is countable: some hard truths. Note the plural is truths /truːðz/ with a voiced th.

entries.meaning: The achievement of a goal; a thing that achieves it.
examples: Success takes far longer than people expect.
He has had some success with the method.
Her success was entirely deserved.
The show was an enormous success.
The program's early successes justified the funding.

senses.head: Achievement generally
examples: Success takes far longer than people expect.
He has had some success with the method.
Her success was entirely deserved.

senses.head: A successful thing or person
examples: The show was an enormous success.
The program's early successes justified the funding.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as achievement generally, countable as a successful thing
entries.agreement: singular for the concept — success takes time; plural for instances — the successes outweighed the failures
entries.counted with: a measure of success
entries.contrast: ✗ He had a success meaning he succeeded is odd; say he was successful or he had some success. A success means a thing that succeeded: the show was a success.

entries.meaning: Lack of success; an instance of it; a breakdown.
examples: Failure is more instructive than success.
Fear of failure stopped him applying.
The launch was a spectacular failure.
Both failures had the same root cause.
He died of heart failure.

senses.head: The concept
examples: Failure is more instructive than success.
Fear of failure stopped him applying.

senses.head: An instance
examples: The launch was a spectacular failure.
Both failures had the same root cause.

senses.head: A breakdown
examples: He died of heart failure.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the concept, countable as an instance
entries.agreement: singular for the concept — failure is instructive; plural for instances — the failures were catalogued
entries.counted with: a case of failure
entries.contrast: Mirrors success exactly. Note the technical sense — engine failure, kidney failure — which is uncountable and very common.

entries.meaning: The emotion of being afraid; a specific thing feared.
examples: Fear is useful right up until it paralyzes you.
He felt no fear at all.
She has a fear of enclosed spaces.
All his fears turned out to be justified.
Both fears proved groundless.

senses.head: The emotion
examples: Fear is useful right up until it paralyzes you.
He felt no fear at all.

senses.head: A specific worry
examples: She has a fear of enclosed spaces.
All his fears turned out to be justified.
Both fears proved groundless.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the emotion, countable as a specific worry
entries.agreement: singular for the emotion — fear is useful; plural for worries — her fears were justified
entries.counted with: a feeling of fear
entries.contrast: The raw emotion is uncountable; a particular thing you are afraid of is countable. He felt fear versus he has a fear of heights — both correct, different grammar.

entries.meaning: The feeling of expectation; a particular thing hoped for.
examples: Hope is not a strategy.
There is still some hope.
She lost all hope after the second rejection.
All her hopes rested on that interview.
Both hopes were dashed within a week.

senses.head: The feeling
examples: Hope is not a strategy.
There is still some hope.
She lost all hope after the second rejection.

senses.head: Particular expectations
examples: All her hopes rested on that interview.
Both hopes were dashed within a week.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the feeling, countable as a specific expectation
entries.agreement: singular for the feeling — hope is not a strategy; plural for expectations — her hopes were dashed
entries.counted with: a glimmer of hope, a ray of hope
entries.contrast: Mirrors fear. The feeling is uncountable; particular expectations are countable and usually plural: my hopes.

entries.meaning: Physical or emotional suffering.
examples: The pain is constant now.
She is in a great deal of pain.
He caused his family real pain.
He had sharp pains in his chest.
Both pains responded to the medication.
That form is a real pain to fill out.

senses.head: Suffering generally
examples: The pain is constant now.
She is in a great deal of pain.
He caused his family real pain.

senses.head: Specific aches
examples: He had sharp pains in his chest.
Both pains responded to the medication.

senses.head: An annoyance
examples: That form is a real pain to fill out.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as sensation, countable as a specific ache
entries.agreement: singular for the sensation — the pain is constant; plural for aches — the pains come and go
entries.counted with: a lot of pain, a twinge of pain
entries.contrast: General suffering is uncountable — she is in pain. Specific localized aches are countable — sharp pains in his chest. Note the idiom a pain meaning an annoying person or thing.

entries.meaning: The faculty of remembering; a single recollection.
examples: Her memory is remarkable for her age.
He recited the whole thing from memory.
It brought back a childhood memory.
All her memories of the place are good.
The phone is out of memory again.

senses.head: The faculty
examples: Her memory is remarkable for her age.
He recited the whole thing from memory.

senses.head: A recollection
examples: It brought back a childhood memory.
All her memories of the place are good.

senses.head: Computer storage
examples: The phone is out of memory again.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the faculty, countable as a recollection
entries.agreement: singular for the faculty — her memory is excellent; plural for recollections — the memories came back
entries.counted with: a feat of memory
entries.contrast: The faculty is uncountable — she has a good memory. A single recollection is countable — a childhood memory. The computer sense is uncountable: the phone is out of memory.

entries.meaning: Ability gained by practice; a particular competence.
examples: It takes real skill to do that cleanly.
He handled the negotiation with great skill.
Her technical skills are in high demand.
The course teaches basic writing skills.
Both skills transfer to almost any job.

senses.head: Ability generally
examples: It takes real skill to do that cleanly.
He handled the negotiation with great skill.

senses.head: A particular competence
examples: Her technical skills are in high demand.
The course teaches basic writing skills.
Both skills transfer to almost any job.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as ability, countable as a particular competence
entries.agreement: singular for ability — skill matters more than luck; plural for competences — her skills are in demand
entries.counted with: a degree of skill, a level of skill
entries.contrast: General ability is uncountable — it takes skill. Particular learned competences are countable — communication skills, and that plural is everywhere in job advertisements.

entries.meaning: Natural ability; a particular gift; also talented people collectively.
examples: Talent is not enough without discipline.
She has enormous talent.
His talents were largely wasted there.
She has a talent for defusing arguments.
The firm is competing for talent with much larger rivals.

senses.head: Natural ability
examples: Talent is not enough without discipline.
She has enormous talent.

senses.head: Particular gifts
examples: His talents were largely wasted there.
She has a talent for defusing arguments.

senses.head: Talented people collectively
examples: The firm is competing for talent with much larger rivals.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as ability, countable as a particular gift
entries.agreement: singular for ability — talent is not enough; plural for gifts — his talents were wasted
entries.counted with: a great deal of talent
entries.contrast: Note the collective use meaning talented people, which is uncountable and takes a singular verb: the company is competing for talent.

entries.meaning: Physical or mental exertion; an organized attempt.
examples: It took a great deal of effort.
He made no effort to hide his boredom.
Relief efforts began within hours.
Both efforts collapsed for lack of funding.
It was a serious effort to reform the system.

senses.head: Exertion
examples: It took a great deal of effort.
He made no effort to hide his boredom.

senses.head: An organized attempt
examples: Relief efforts began within hours.
Both efforts collapsed for lack of funding.
It was a serious effort to reform the system.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as exertion, countable as an attempt
entries.agreement: singular for exertion — effort counts; plural for attempts — their efforts failed
entries.counted with: a great deal of effort
entries.contrast: Exertion is uncountable — it took a lot of effort. Organized attempts are countable — relief efforts, an effort to reform the system.

entries.meaning: The end of life; an instance of dying.
examples: Death comes to everyone eventually.
He showed no fear of death.
Three deaths were reported that week.
Both deaths remain unexplained.
Her death changed the whole family.

senses.head: The concept
examples: Death comes to everyone eventually.
He showed no fear of death.

senses.head: An instance
examples: Three deaths were reported that week.
Both deaths remain unexplained.
Her death changed the whole family.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the concept, countable as an instance
entries.agreement: singular for the concept — death comes to everyone; plural for instances — the deaths were investigated
entries.counted with: a case of death is unnatural — use a death
entries.contrast: The abstract concept takes no article — death is inevitable. Individual deaths are fully countable — three deaths were reported. Note the plural is /dɛθs/ with a voiceless th, unlike truths.

entries.meaning: The system of rules; an individual rule or principle.
examples: She studied law at Michigan.
Law is slow to catch up with technology.
He is above the law, apparently.
Three new laws took effect in January.
The law was repealed after two years.
Newton's laws of motion still hold at ordinary speeds.

senses.head: The system
examples: She studied law at Michigan.
Law is slow to catch up with technology.
He is above the law, apparently.

senses.head: An individual statute
examples: Three new laws took effect in January.
The law was repealed after two years.

senses.head: A scientific principle
examples: Newton's laws of motion still hold at ordinary speeds.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the system, countable as an individual statute
entries.agreement: singular for the system — law is slow to change; plural for statutes — the laws were repealed
entries.counted with: a body of law, a point of law
entries.contrast: The system is uncountable and takes no article — she studies law, never ✗ a law in that sense. Individual statutes and scientific principles are countable.

entries.meaning: Systematic knowledge of the natural world; a branch of it.
examples: Science advances by argument, not consensus.
She teaches science to ninth graders.
The natural sciences are funded separately.
Economics is a social science.
Hiring is not an exact science.

senses.head: The field
examples: Science advances by argument, not consensus.
She teaches science to ninth graders.

senses.head: A branch of it
examples: The natural sciences are funded separately.
Economics is a social science.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: Hiring is not an exact science.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the field, countable as a discipline
entries.agreement: singular for the field — science advances by argument; plural for disciplines — the sciences are separately funded
entries.counted with: a branch of science
entries.contrast: The activity is uncountable — she studies science. Individual disciplines are countable — the natural sciences, an exact science. The idiom it's not an exact science means it involves judgment.

entries.meaning: The past; the study of it; a written account.
examples: History is written by the winners, supposedly.
He teaches American history.
She wrote a history of the canal.
The two histories disagree on almost everything.
The doctor took a full medical history.

senses.head: The past and its study
examples: History is written by the winners, supposedly.
He teaches American history.

senses.head: A written account
examples: She wrote a history of the canal.
The two histories disagree on almost everything.

senses.head: A personal record
examples: The doctor took a full medical history.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the subject, countable as an account or record
entries.agreement: singular for the subject — history is written by the winners; plural for accounts — the histories disagree
entries.counted with: a period of history
entries.contrast: The subject is uncountable — he teaches history. A written account is countable — a history of Rome. A personal record is also countable: a medical history.

entries.meaning: The human capacity for speech; a particular tongue; a style of expression.
examples: Language is what most clearly separates us.
The origins of language remain contested.
She speaks four languages fluently.
Both languages are official here.
The letter contained some very strong language.

senses.head: The human faculty
examples: Language is what most clearly separates us.
The origins of language remain contested.

senses.head: A particular tongue
examples: She speaks four languages fluently.
Both languages are official here.

senses.head: A style of expression
examples: The letter contained some very strong language.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the human faculty, countable as a particular tongue
entries.agreement: singular for the faculty — language is uniquely human; plural for tongues — both languages are spoken here
entries.counted with: a form of language
entries.contrast: The human capacity is uncountable — the origins of language. Individual tongues are countable — she speaks four languages. A style of expression is uncountable: strong language.

entries.meaning: The activity of thinking; an individual idea.
examples: Give it some thought before you decide.
Thought requires a certain amount of quiet.
I had a thought about the schedule.
His thoughts were clearly elsewhere.
The book surveys modern economic thought.

senses.head: The activity
examples: Give it some thought before you decide.
Thought requires a certain amount of quiet.

senses.head: An individual idea
examples: I had a thought about the schedule.
His thoughts were clearly elsewhere.

senses.head: A body of ideas
examples: The book surveys modern economic thought.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the activity, countable as an individual idea
entries.agreement: singular for the activity — thought requires quiet; plural for ideas — his thoughts were elsewhere
entries.counted with: a train of thought
entries.contrast: The activity of thinking is uncountable — give it some thought. An individual idea is countable — I had a thought. Note also the sense meaning a school of ideas: modern economic thought.

entries.meaning: Uncertainty; a particular reservation.
examples: There is no doubt about what happened.
Doubt crept in about halfway through.
Beyond reasonable doubt is the legal standard.
I have my doubts about the timeline.
Both doubts turned out to be well founded.

senses.head: Uncertainty generally
examples: There is no doubt about what happened.
Doubt crept in about halfway through.
Beyond reasonable doubt is the legal standard.

senses.head: Particular reservations
examples: I have my doubts about the timeline.
Both doubts turned out to be well founded.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the state, countable as a specific reservation
entries.agreement: singular for the state — doubt crept in; plural for reservations — her doubts grew
entries.counted with: a shadow of doubt, an element of doubt
entries.contrast: The b is silent, as in debt and subtle. General uncertainty is uncountable — there is no doubt. Particular reservations are countable and usually plural — I have my doubts.

entries.meaning: Accountability; a specific duty.
examples: He took full responsibility for the error.
Responsibility comes with the job.
Her responsibilities include hiring.
Both responsibilities fell to the same person.
It is not my responsibility to fix that.

senses.head: Accountability
examples: He took full responsibility for the error.
Responsibility comes with the job.

senses.head: A specific duty
examples: Her responsibilities include hiring.
Both responsibilities fell to the same person.
It is not my responsibility to fix that.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the quality, countable as a specific duty
entries.agreement: singular for the quality — responsibility comes with the job; plural for duties — her responsibilities grew
entries.counted with: a sense of responsibility
entries.contrast: Being accountable is uncountable — he takes responsibility. Specific duties are countable — my responsibilities include payroll.

entries.meaning: A favorable set of circumstances; a specific chance.
examples: Opportunity is very unevenly distributed.
The city offers real opportunity.
She had the opportunity to study abroad.
Both opportunities came at the wrong time.
Job opportunities dried up that year.

senses.head: Favorable conditions
examples: Opportunity is very unevenly distributed.
The city offers real opportunity.

senses.head: A specific chance
examples: She had the opportunity to study abroad.
Both opportunities came at the wrong time.
Job opportunities dried up that year.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as favorable conditions, countable as a specific chance
entries.agreement: singular for conditions — opportunity is unevenly distributed; plural for chances — the opportunities dried up
entries.counted with: a window of opportunity
entries.contrast: ✗ I have a possibility to go is a very common error — English says an opportunity to go or a chance to go. Possibility means something that might be true, not something you can do.

entries.meaning: Risk of harm; a specific hazard.
examples: She was in real danger for several hours.
Danger is simply part of the job.

There is a danger that nobody will notice.

senses.head: The state of risk
examples: She was in real danger for several hours.
Danger is simply part of the job.

senses.head: A specific hazard
examples: The dangers of the route were obvious.
Both dangers had been flagged in advance.
There is a danger that nobody will notice.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the state, countable as a specific hazard
entries.agreement: singular for the state — danger is part of the job; plural for hazards — the dangers were obvious
entries.counted with: a degree of danger
entries.contrast: Being at risk is uncountable — she is in danger. Specific hazards are countable — the dangers of the route.

entries.meaning: The state of being hard; a specific problem.
examples: He had difficulty breathing.
The difficulty increases with each level.

senses.head: The quality
examples: He had difficulty breathing.
The difficulty increases with each level.
She found the exam of moderate difficulty.

senses.head: A specific problem
examples: We ran into technical difficulties.
Both difficulties were resolved by lunchtime.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the quality, countable as a specific problem
entries.agreement: singular for the quality — difficulty varies; plural for problems — the difficulties multiplied
entries.counted with: a degree of difficulty
entries.contrast: The quality of being hard is uncountable — he had difficulty breathing. Specific problems are countable — technical difficulties.

entries.meaning: Enjoyment; a source of enjoyment.
examples: She takes real pleasure in gardening.
Pleasure is not the same thing as happiness.

senses.head: The feeling
examples: She takes real pleasure in gardening.
Pleasure is not the same thing as happiness.
It was a pleasure to meet you.

senses.head: A source of enjoyment
examples: The simple pleasures are the ones that last.
Both pleasures were entirely legal.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the feeling, countable as a source of it
entries.agreement: singular for the feeling — pleasure is not the same as happiness; plural for sources — simple pleasures are the best
entries.counted with: a source of pleasure
entries.contrast: The feeling is uncountable — she takes pleasure in it. A thing that gives pleasure is countable — the simple pleasures of a Sunday.

examples: She travels in considerable comfort.

senses.head: Physical ease or consolation
examples: She travels in considerable comfort.
His presence was a great comfort.
There is cold comfort in being proved right.

senses.head: A comforting thing
examples: The small comforts of home are what you miss.
Both comforts were stripped from the budget.

entries.countability: both — uncountable as the state, countable as a comforting thing
entries.agreement: singular for the state — comfort matters; plural for things — the small comforts of home
entries.counted with: a degree of comfort
entries.contrast: Physical ease and consolation are uncountable. Particular comforting things are countable and usually plural: creature comforts.
